chapters.label: Story 1
chapters.title: A Quiet Evening
paras: Clara Vance came home early on a Thursday after the dentist had cancelled their appointment. She entered through the side door that opened into the hall beside the coat hooks, and was already talking as she bent to unbuckle her shoes.

“They rang me in the car park, Tom. Can you believe it? I’d sat there for about twenty minutes reading a magazine about yachts.” She set the shoes side by side on the mat, heel to heel, as she always did.
“You know what, I’ve decided I want a yacht.”
There was no response, which was unusual. Tom was supposed to be home.
Under the hum of the fridge there was a second hum, wet and uneven, like someone breathing through a cloth.

She went down the hall in her stockinged feet, treading cautiously on the cool boards. At the kitchen doorway, her toes became wet. She looked down and saw that it was not the shadow of the doorframe on the tiles, as she had thought, but a dark flat spread of red, growing slowly over the tidy squares of the kitchen tiles.
Then she lifted her eyes.

The kitchen was normal; how it always was. There was a bottle of honey on the cupboard, and the window over the sink blew in the scent of the neighbour’s sycamore. The radio on the windowsill was playing something low with violins. The kettle had boiled and clicked off and two mugs stood beside it with the teabags already in. One of them was hers, the blue one with the chip on the handle.
But amongst all this ordinariness lay a woman, flat on her back in the space between the table and the cooker.

She was around fifty and wore an expensive cream trouser suit. One of her shoes had come off and lay on its side under a chair like a small animal, crept away to hide. Her hair was dyed the even red of expensive mahogany furniture. Her eyes were open and fixed on the light fitting with an expression of mild offence. The front of her jacket was torn in five or six places, close together, over the heart, each with a dark clean cut. The whole front of her cloth had gone black and heavy with blood.

Her husband, Tom, stood over the woman, holding a bloodied knife. His sleeves were rolled to the elbow, and the front of the shirt was stained with blood. He was looking at the woman’s face and did not seem to have heard Clara come in, and then, slowly, his head turned.

She had been married to him for eleven years but she couldn’t read the expression on his face. First his mouth opened but nothing came out, and then he wanted to laugh but stopped. Then his face crumpled and his eyes filled, and he put his free hand over them like a boy caught with his hand in the cookie jar, then he took it away and looked at it, then at the knife. He then set the knife on the counter very carefully, squaring it to the edge.
“Clara,” he said. “Clara…” He said it as if he were trying to remember what he had planned to say.

He went to the sink and turned the tap on full and held his hands under it, and the water ran pink and then clear. He turned the tap off, then turned it on again, then began to say the Lord’s Prayer in a fast flat mumble, then stopped halfway through and turned round, his breathing all over the place.

Clara looked at the dead woman. She looked at the red hair, the small gold hoops in her ears, and the left hand lying palm up on the tiles with three rings on it, one of them a signet, a flat oval black stone. She knew that ring.
The radio finished the song with the violins and the news turned to sports announcements.
“I’m going to go out,” Clara said.
Her voice came from somewhere slightly above and to the left of her head. It sounded perfectly ordinary, like how she had said she was leaving too this morning.

Tom stared at her but did not move towards her. He did not ask her where, or why, or say wait. His hands hung at his sides dripping on the floor, and his lips moved, but nothing came out this time either.

She went back down the hall, put her shoes on, the left and then the right, and buckled them. Her fingers were steady. When she was fine, she took her bag from the hook and her keys from the bowl, and let herself out by the side door then closed it behind her, quietly, as if not to wake a sleeping child.

She drove to the river. There was a lay-by on the Old Mill Road where the bank fell away under willows and the water moved brown and quick between the stones. In summer people parked there to eat chips with the windows down. Today there was nobody. Clara turned off the engine and sat with her hands on the wheel at ten and two, as she had been taught, and listened to the engine tick as it cooled down.
She did not cry or feel anything, and noticed that she did not, and noticed her noticing, and she let it all go by.

What she thought about instead was the flat above a launderette in a city she had not visited in nineteen years. The smell of fabric conditioner coming up through the floorboards day and night, sweet as a sickroom. A radiator that knocked, a door with three locks on the outside, and a redheaded woman who wore a black signet ring that left a small oval bruise when she held your wrist to stop you going anywhere and who brought them takeaway on Sundays and called them her girls.

Clara had been nineteen when she got out. She had got out by escaping into a laundry van, and the driver had pretended not to see her when she climbed in among the sacks and had said nothing for two hundred miles except, once, when they stopped at a petrol station, and he’d turned and said, “Hey, you there, want some coffee?” She had never learned his name and had changed hers soon after. She had met Tom later at a friend’s wedding, where he had spilled champagne down her dress and then spent the rest of the evening trying to get it out with soda water, genuinely distressed. She had married him soon after because he was good and kind and was in some way the least frightening man she had ever met.
She had never told him much about those days, just about the woman, once when she’d seen her face online…
A heron came down on the far bank, folded itself and stood there, grey and patient, looking into the river like it was philosophising.
Clara watched it until the sun began to go down. Then she started the car, drove into town and parked behind the market.

The Lebanese place on Fenner Street was just turning its sign. She stood at the counter under the strip light and placed her order: lamb with pomegranate, the chicken shish, fattoush, hummus, the flatbreads that came wrapped in paper, a tray of baklava… all Tom’s favourites. The young man behind the counter asked if she was celebrating something.
“You could say that,” she said.
He laughed and put in extra pickles for free.
The bag was warm against her side all the way to the car. It smelled of cumin, charcoal, and garlic, and she held it on her lap at the traffic lights and found that she was simply now hungry.
It was fully dark when she pulled into the driveway. The porch light was on. The kitchen blind was down and lit gold from behind.
She did not use her key. When she arrived, she stood on the step with the bag in her arms and knocked, twice.

She heard him coming down the hall, and then the door opened and there he was, in the blue jumper she had bought him for Christmas, his hair still damp and combed flat from the shower, his face pink with heat. He smelled of lime soap. Behind him the hall floor gleamed.
“There you are,” he smiled. It was a genuine smile. “I was starting to wonder. Why are you knocking, you daft little thing? Did you lose your keys?”
“My hands were full,” she said.
“Give that here.” He took the bag and looked in it and groaned. “Oh, you angel. Fenner Street? On a Thursday?”
“I thought you deserved it.”
He kissed her on the cheek, just beside her ear, and carried the bag down the hall ahead of her. She shut the door and followed him into the kitchen.

It was her usual kitchen. The tiles were all white, even the grout between them was sparkling white, but it smelled of bleach under a fierce lemon that made her eyes sting. The window was open an inch and the chairs were tucked under the table. The knife he had used earlier was not on the counter, nor in the block; the slot where it lived stood empty, a small dark mouth. Both mugs had been washed and put away and the radio was off. Somewhere in the house the washing machine was turning over in its long spin, a deep steady thrum she could feel in the soles of her feet.

Tom laid the table and did it properly, which he rarely did: placemats, the good plates, cloth napkins from the drawer. He found the candle in the cupboard over the fridge and lit it with a match and stood it in a saucer in the middle, then unpacked the food into bowls instead of eating it from the cartons. He hummed while he did it all. It was the song from the radio, she realised, the one from that afternoon with the violins.
“Sit,” he said, pulling out her chair. “Sit, sit. You’ve been on your feet all through the day.”
She sat.

They ate. The lamb was soft enough to cut with a fork. Tom tore the flatbread, dragged it through the hummus, and closed his eyes when he chewed, the way he did with things he loved. She talked about a man at her office who earlier that morning had brought his tortoise in because he said it felt lonely at home. He asked her opinion on whether she thought tortoises could be lonely and she said she thought anything alive could.
“So, how was your day?” she asked.
“Oh,” he said, and shrugged, and reached for the pickles. “Fine… Okay, I guess. Normal and boring really.”
“So dry. Nothing happened?” she queried.

“Nothing worth anything.” He crunched a pickle and pointed the rest of it at her. “I’ll be honest, I had a bit of a moment this afternoon. I was all over the place. Couldn’t think straight. But you know how things are… got it sorted out.” He shook his head, smiling at himself. “Stress, I suppose. But I’m all right now.” He looked at her across the candle.
“Good,” Clara said. “I guess it’s just stress. You should try to be resting well.”
He nodded.
“How was the dentist?” he asked.
“Cancelled on me again. I made a short stop at home and left almost immediately.”
“Typical of them.” He passed her the baklava. “So what did you do with yourself?”
“I went by the river for the nice view.”
“Liked it?”
She thought about the heron. “Very peaceful,” she said.

He nodded as though that was exactly the answer he had expected. The washing machine reached the end of its spin, then shuddered and went quiet. In the quiet she could hear the candle burning, a tiny fluttering sound, the tick-tock of the clock in the hall, and his breathing, which was slow, easy, and even.

Afterwards he would not let her help with the dishes. She sat at the cleared table with her hands round a cup of mint tea and watched his back as he washed up, the jumper pulled tight across his shoulders, the water steaming.

Upstairs he drew the curtains and turned down her side of the bed first, which he had done every night since their honeymoon and which she had never once mentioned to him in case he became self-conscious and stopped.

She brushed her teeth, took off her watch and earrings and laid them in their little china dish. The pale ridge on her wrist caught the light and she looked at it for a while before she turned off the bathroom light.

They lay down on their backs in the dark, side by side, not touching. The radiator ticked as it cooled. A car went by outside, and its headlights swung across the ceiling, a long bar of light that slid from one corner to the other and was gone.
“Tom,” she said.
“Mm?”
“Thank you.”
He was quiet. She heard him turn his head on the pillow towards her. She did not turn hers and kept her eyes on the ceiling where the light had been.
“I love you,” she said.
His hand found hers under the duvet. It was very warm and slightly damp, and held on hard, then eased.
“I love you too,” he said. His voice was thick. He cleared his throat. “I’ll always keep you safe, Clara. Always. You know that, don’t you?”
“I know.”
“Nothing’s ever going to get to you. Not ever again.”
After a while his breathing lengthened, his grip slackened, and his thumb, which had been moving back and forth across her knuckles, went still.

Clara reached over to the bedside table and found her phone, then turned it on under the edge of the duvet so the light would not wake him. Her own face, lit blue, would have looked to anyone like the face of a woman checking for something casual.

She opened her messages. Her sister had sent a photograph of a cake. A friend wanted to know about her plan for Saturday. She scrolled with her thumb until a banner dropped down from the top of the screen.
BREAKING: Body found in River Leane identified as Vera Sokol, 51, sought for two decades over trafficking network
She pressed it to read.

The body had been recovered at a quarter past seven that evening by two men fishing below the weir at Old Mill. Police had confirmed the identity from fingerprints held on an international database. Sokol had been the subject of arrest warrants in four countries in connection with the trafficking of young women for sexual exploitation. She had died following multiple stab wounds to the chest, seemingly from someone trying to escape her clutches. Officers were appealing to the public for any witnesses.

Further down there was a quote from a detective chief inspector. We will investigate this death with the same thoroughness as any other, he had said, and then, the article noted, he had thought long and hard before adding, I won’t pretend this is a straightforward case for this department. I’m not sure tonight whether I’m meant to find the perpetrator responsible for this crime to arrest them or to shake their hand.
Below that, the comments had already started pouring in. Clara read them slowly, one after another, with the duvet pulled up to her chin and her husband asleep beside her.

Women with no photographs and first names only, writing from other cities and countries, in English that was sometimes not their first language had started to send in their stories. I was fifteen when… Whoever you are, thank you. And again and again, copied from one to the next like a password, the same three words: rightly deserved justice.
Clara read until the screen dimmed itself.

Then she turned the phone face down on the table and lay back. Beside her Tom murmured something in his sleep and rolled towards her, and his arm came over her, heavy and warm, the clean blue wool of his jumper against her cheek, and, so faint that she might have imagined it, the smell of bleach.

She closed her eyes. Downstairs the clean kitchen stayed in the dark with a knife missing from the block. Down the road and across the fields the river went on in the night, carrying what it had been given towards the sea.
For the first time in nineteen years, Clara Vance closed her eyes and slept peacefully.

chapters.label: Story 2
chapters.title: Twenty Houses Down
paras: I counted them once, afterwards. I walked up the hill from my house to his on a Sunday when the street was empty and counted every gate. Twenty. Nineteen houses between his and mine, with a bend in the road where the pavement changes from cracked concrete to clean pale stone, and a jacaranda that drops its purple on both of us.

Rua das Laranjeiras goes down the hill like flowing water. At the top of the neighbourhood, the houses are nice estates with walls, gates, and gardens. At the bottom, where I live, it is a ghetto, no walls or gardens, only doors that open straight into the street, the smell of everybody’s cooking, and a drain that floods in March. People at the top drive down the street on their way. People at the bottom walk up it on their way.

My daughter Nina was six years old during the winter when she got sick. It began as a cough but later developed into something serious. So serious that there were some words I had to ask the doctor to write down so I could buy the drugs he prescribed. The medicine I had to buy next was one that came in a small white box from another country, twelve doses to a box, and cost more than I earned in four months of loading lorries at the depot.
I sold what I had to afford it. It was not much. The television, my father’s watch, our gas cooker, so we started cooking with charcoal on our doorstep.
My wife Rosa took in sewing until her fingers bled at the tips, but she wrapped them and carried on until we bought one box.
Nina took the doses and was soon revived. But soon, the box was empty, and by the end of the second week she was once more on the verge of death.

But there was a house at the top of the street with a blue door that I’d been looking at. I had noticed it because it seemed the least secure, so I figured the owner must be rich and not care if some of what they had went missing.

It was also the only house with no car outside in the day. Most of the rich houses had two cars, one that left and one that stayed. The blue-door house had one, an old green Mercedes, beautifully kept, and it left every morning at half past seven and came back every evening after dark. No children’s toys in the garden. No dog. A woman’s sun hat on a hook on the porch that never moved, so nobody had worn it in a long time.
I had never stolen anything in my life except, when I was nine, some mangos from a market stall, and I was so sick with shame that I stole away to give them back and got caught.

I went up the street on a Wednesday afternoon in a borrowed overall with a toolbag, so that if anyone saw me they would think I had come about the drains. The jacaranda was shedding, so my shoes left marks in the purple.

The gate of the blue-door house was not electric, which was a delight. It had a latch, which lifted when I pried it open. The back door had a pane of frosted glass. So I wrapped my elbow in my jacket and gave it a clean tap and the glass gave way.

Inside it was cool, dim, and smelled of floor polish, old books and something medical that I knew from the clinic. I did not look at much. I could not. My heart was fluttering about. I went through the kitchen and the hall into a bedroom with a big wardrobe of dark wood, and opened the wardrobe because that is where my own mother kept the good stuff, and on the top shelf, behind a row of folded sweaters, was a biscuit tin. A blue tin with a picture of a Scottish castle on the lid.
It was heavy.
I did not open it there. I put it in the toolbag and went out the way I had come and closed the latch behind me, then walked down the hill as casually as I could muster.
At home I opened the tin can at the table with the shutters closed. Rosa stood behind me with her injured fingers over her mouth.

It was money. The tin was full of money. Notes in bundles with paper bands round them, the bands written on in pencil in a small neat hand: a date and an amount, a date and an amount, going back years. Some of the earliest bands were soft and furred with handling. On top of the bundles lay a folded sheet of paper. I did not unfold it. I simply put it back in the tin and closed the lid on it, because I didn’t want to grow a conscience, not for my baby’s sake.
And luckily, the money was enough for eleven boxes, surgery, and life after.

Nina got better and she grew healthier. By Easter she was back at school, and by June she was running around the street with the other children, shrieking, her plaits flying, and I would stand in the doorway and watch her and be glad I did all I could as a father should.

The man from the blue-door house… I saw him once more at the top of the hill, in those weeks after I’d taken the tin can. He was standing at his gate in the evening with his hands at his sides, not moving. He was tall and grey, perhaps sixty, in a good jacket that hung on him as if it had belonged to someone bigger. He would do nothing but stand at the gate, looking at his door, and I would walk past on the other side of the road with my head down and my hands in my pockets.

In August, the green Mercedes was gone from outside the blue door. In October, there was a sign on the gate. Vende-se. And in November, on a Saturday morning, a small removal van came grinding down the hill in first gear with its brakes squealing and stopped outside the house next door to mine, which had been empty since old Senhora Castro died, a single room with a tin roof and a small toilet.

Two young men carried in a bed frame, a mattress, one armchair, a kitchen table, four boxes, and a tall dark wooden wardrobe that would not go through the door until they took the door off its hinges.
The man from the blue-door house got out of the cab, stood in the street and looked at the little room for a long time, then he went in.

His name was Teodoro Abreu. He came out on his first evening to sit on the step of his room, because there was nowhere to sit inside but the bed and one armchair, and because the evening was warm, and I was sitting on my step next to him with a beer and a metre of pavement between us.
“Good evening,” he said.
“Good evening.”
“I’m Teodoro. I’ve just moved in.”
“Elias,” I said. “Welcome.”

He nodded. He looked at the street, at the children chasing a football through the puddles from the burst main, at the woman opposite shouting at her husband about something. He had a way of looking at things very carefully. You could tell he was observant.
“It’s lively down here,” he said.
“You get used to it.”
“I’m sure.” He smiled. It was a thin smile but a real one. “I’ve got nothing else to get used to.”

I offered him a beer. I don’t know why. My hand just did it. It was the least I could do. He took it and thanked me and we drank. That was the first evening I ever spoke to him and there were many more.

He was a kind, quiet man and he once helped fix Nina’s bicycle chain with a pair of pliers and a great deal of patience, then taught her how to do it herself, and she adored him at once. He also lent Rosa his iron when ours broke and had a radio, which in the evenings played old music, sambas from before I was born, with the volume low, with him sitting on his step with his eyes closed. On Sundays he went somewhere on the bus, in his good jacket, and came back looking sad, and went straight inside.
I knew the man and I loved him terribly like a brother, which made it harder to look him in the eyes.

Every night that I lay beside Rosa and listened to Nina breathing in the next bed, I would be grateful, but on the other side of the wall I could hear Teodoro turning over in his narrow bed, the springs squeaking, and I would hate myself.
It was a night in January, very hot, with the air full of insects, when I asked him.

We had been sitting a long time, the street had gone quiet and Nina was already asleep. Someone up the hill was having a party; we could hear it faintly, the noise, coming down to us over the rooftops like the smell of food.
“Teodoro,” I said. “Can I ask you something?”
“Of course.”
“Why did you move here?” I looked at my bottle. “A man like you. You talk educated. You got a nice jacket. You don’t belong here. So why you here living small at the bottom of Laranjeiras?”
He was quiet for so long that I thought he had not heard me. Then he put his bottle down very carefully on the step, as if it might go off.
“I lived up there,” he said, and nodded up the hill. “At the top… the house with the blue door. You know it?”
“I seen it,” I said.

“My father bought it.” He smiled in the dark. “He was a tram driver. Forty years he drove the number nine and saved every cent he could for thirty of those years to buy that house for my mother and me. He bought it in the spring, and in the autumn he died. Heart gave out. He never really got to live in it. But I grew up there. My mother died there too. And then I brought my wife there, Lúcia, and we lived there thirty-one years. My father left me his car too… early wedding present.” He laughed softly. “He loved that car more than he loved me… told me himself. Said he’ll haunt me if it got scratched. So I kept it the way he kept it. Every Saturday, polished the hell off it.”
I did not say anything. I could not.

“Then Lúcia got sick,” he said. “Three years ago. Her heart, just like my father. They told us she needed a new one. A transplant. There’s a list, you know… a long list. And a great deal of money that has to be found before they even put your name near the top. Money for the operation, the tests, the medicines after, which you take your whole life.” He spread his hands. “I’m a schoolteacher. History. Never had a great deal of money, so I saved. I took extra classes, tutored some rich kids in the evenings. I stopped buying books, put it all away in an old biscuit tin, because I don’t trust banks; my father didn’t either. Every month, a little bundle… looking at it grow gave me hope, you know…”
The music up the hill stopped and started again.

“Last April it was close enough,” he said. “Finally. I went to the hospital and they said to bring it in and they could schedule her for an assessment. I went home in the middle of the day to get it. I was so happy I bought her flowers on the way, lilies… she always loved lilies. I came in and noticed that the glass in the back door was broken.”
He stopped and sat very still.

“Someone had taken it all,” he said. “All that I’d kept to use to save my… thing is, I had a letter in that tin too that I wrote to Lúcia for after the operation, for her to read. Some silly love letter.” He shook his head. “I still think about that letter. I wonder if whoever took it read it and if they laughed?”
I could not breathe.

“So I sold the car,” he said simply. “Then sold the house… but it wasn’t enough. The prices went up while I was trying. She’s currently in the hospital across the river now, on a machine. I see her on Sundays… but now she’s not even conscious…” He picked up his beer and looked at it then put it down. “I’ve stopped hoping, Elias, that’s the truth.”
The insects ticked against the street lamp.
And I spilled. “It was me.”
He turned his head.
“It was me,” I said. “The tin… The blue tin with the image of a castle. I broke the glass with my elbow and took it from the top of your wardrobe behind the sweaters.”

My voice had gone strange, high and cracked like a boy’s. I could not stop it. “My daughter… Nina… Her heart was failing. She needed medicine and I couldn’t pay for it… She was dying, Teodoro.” I had my hands over my face. “I didn’t read the letter… I swear to God, I didn’t open it. It’s still in the tin… I kept the tin, I couldn’t throw it away. I’m sorry… I’m really sorry.”

I don’t know how long I sat there with my face in my hands. I heard him breathing, with the partying still happening up the hill. I waited for him to stand, shout, to punch me, or to leave and head for the police station.
When I took my hands away he was looking at me. His face was wet now, but he was not angry. The nearest word I have ever found for what it was is tired.
“Elias,” he said. “It’s all right.”
“It’s not.”

“It is.” He reached across the metre of pavement and put his hand on my knee, and his hand was shaking. “Listen to me, Elias. If I had been you and it had been my child, I would have done the same. I’m sure of it.”
“Then why didn’t you?” I said. It came out of me before I could stop it. “You were desperate too.”
He took his hand back and thought about it.
“Because I didn’t have the courage,” he said. “To choose to hurt someone else, to make my own pain go away.”
Lúcia Abreu died on a Sunday in March, during the rains, when the drain at the bottom of the street flooded and we had to put bricks in front of our doors.

He was with her and returned on the last bus, soaked to the skin. I went out and sat beside him. Neither of us said anything. After a while Rosa came out with a blanket and put it round both of us, and after a while longer Nina came out in her nightdress and squeezed in between us then fell asleep against his arm with her mouth open, and he sat very still so as not to wake her.
I gave him the tin the next morning. The letter was still in it, folded inside. He took it out and looked at it for a long time and then put it in the inside pocket of his good jacket.

He lives there still, in the room next to mine. I don’t know how many years it has been now. He taught Nina all the history she knows, and when she went up the hill last year to sit her examinations at the good school at the top, it was Teodoro who walked her there and waited outside until she came out. He calls her his granddaughter and he’s practically family; she calls him Vô.
Rosa sets a place for him at our table every night and on Sundays he takes the bus across the river with a bunch of lilies to his wife’s grave, and on some Sundays I go with him.

We sit on our steps in the evenings with a metre of pavement between us and listen to his old music with the volume low. Sometimes the people from the top of the hill go by in their cars on their way to somewhere else. Sometimes the jacaranda drops its flowers on both of us.
And every so often, when it is very late and the street is quiet, he will say, without looking at me, “Did you really not read it?”
And I will say, “I swear it.”
And he will nod and say, “Good. It was a very terrible letter.” And we will laugh, two old men on two steps, twenty houses down.
